answer.answer:
**Summary**

A robot can build when four things are present at once: a machine that can reach and hold, a plan for where to move it, work packaged so it can be handled (prefabricated, standardised components), and an organisation whose delivery model and work culture will carry it. The plan is not free: path planning needs 3D geometry and onboard localisation, and it is constrained indoors where satellite positioning is unreliable. Where people share the workspace, collaborative operation rests on a trained workforce and on compliance with robot safety standards, with force-limited operation the single cited route to reducing contact injury. The payoff, on the evidence here, is schedule compression, fewer errors and real economic benefit on geometrically complex work, and four deployed Japanese assembly processes are recorded at technology readiness level 9.

**Detailed answer**

Retrieval widened "robot" to the robot arm, robotic assembly, unmanned mobile vehicles and gantry systems, and "build" to automated production workflow, path planning, remote control and human-robot interaction; the load-bearing evidence sits on robotic assembly (PR4) and path planning (PR12), so that is where the answer is anchored.

**What robotic assembly requires.** PR4 carries exactly 4 inbound and 6 outbound dependency edges, so this list of preconditions is complete as coded:

- **A robot arm (RE2).** Robot arm (RE2) enables robotic assembly (PR4): a robot arm enables robotic assembly [1], backed by peer-reviewed evidence [7], and the graph also records the converse dependency, PR4 dependsOn RE2, robotic assembly requires a robot arm [2] [1].
- **Path planning (PR12).** Path planning (PR12) enables robotic assembly (PR4): path planning is a precondition for robotic assembly [3] [2].
- **Standardised prefabricated components (AT7).** AT7 enablesCapability PR4: Japanese automated erection systems rely on standardised prefabricated components [2] [1]. Alongside it, PR4 hasPrecondition PR2: automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials [2] [1].
- **An all-weather cover (CO12).** CO12 enablesCapability PR4: all-weather cover allows welding and assembly to proceed in a normal manner even in rain [2] [1].
- **An organisational context (RI12).** This is a directional dependency, not a correlation: robotic assembly (PR4) depends on delivery model, business model and work culture (RI12), because robotics adoption in precast production rests on the environmental and organisational context [4] [9]. RI12 is activated in 16 of the 50 coded cases.

**What path planning in turn requires.** PR12 carries exactly 3 inbound and 3 outbound edges. Inbound: AI/deep reinforcement learning (RE8) enables autonomous path planning [2] and algorithmic geometry (RE1) drives toolpath and path generation [2] [1]. Outbound, beyond PR4: PR12 dependsOn CO16, path planning requires 3D point-cloud geometry [2], and PR12 hasPrecondition RE4, localisation via onboard sensors as a fundamental prerequisite for autonomous operation [2] [1]. One constraint is coded against it: RI5 constrains PR12, since reliable GNSS signals are typically unavailable indoors, constraining localisation method choice [2] [1]. PR12 is activated in 26 of the 50 coded cases, PR4 in only 13.

**Where people are in the workspace.** Human-robot collaboration (CO6, activated in 32 of 50 cases) carries 0 inbound and 3 outbound edges, all dependencies of its own: CO6 dependsOn RI6, because success of human-robot collaboration is contingent on a skilled workforce, so it depends on addressing workforce training [2]; CO6 dependsOn RI18, human-robot collaborative work depends on compliance with robot safety standards [2] (standards evidence); and CO6 mitigates RI20, power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation within biomechanical limits mitigates contact-injury risk [2] [1].

**The automated production workflow behind it.** AR9 is activated in 44 of 50 coded cases, the second most common enabler retrieved here. It is enabled by fabrication information modelling linking BIM-based design to digital fabrication via a digital chain (CO3) [2], by manufacturing information generated independently of the machine system (RE13) [2], and by integrated information management for integrated automated construction (RE9) [2]; it in turn dependsOn RI6, since high sophistication of digital technologies prohibits adoption by less technologically familiar workers and skills and training are required [2], and enables VA1, reducing dependence on site labour in response to labour shortage and ageing [2] [1].

**What it returns.** Robotic assembly amplifies time efficiency (VA2): productivity is higher when the robotic method is used for geometrically complex walls [5] [8]; PR4 enablesCapability VA10, robotic and factory assembly reduces errors [2]; and PR4 amplifies VA6, with cost and time analysis showing significant economic benefit for geometrically complex walls [2] [1]. VA2 is activated in 49 of the 50 coded cases. Note that VA2's other strong links here, for example with RE6 in 49 cases and VA1 in 48, are co-occurrence only, statistical association rather than asserted dependency.

**Deployed record.** Four census processes in front of me perform assembly, all at technology readiness level 9: census_RXH1-1, adopted to address integration, performing assembly, steelwork and welding on the structural core and the building envelope [6]
